I handle customer support at our tiffin-subscription startup, so I heard the pricing fight from my desk for two weeks. Kavitha wanted ₹2,400 a month; Tarun wanted ₹2,900. Every afternoon, the same argument, a little louder.
Then one Monday they stopped. Kavitha wrote on the whiteboard: "Test, 3 weeks. New customers in Andheri see ₹2,400. New customers in Powai see ₹2,900. Whichever brings in more money with fewer cancellations wins. We both follow it." Tarun signed his name under it, and so did she.
For three weeks I tagged every signup by area in the sheet. Nobody argued. At the end, the higher price had slightly fewer signups but more money and about the same cancellations. Tarun's price won. Kavitha looked at the result for a long moment, then said, "Okay. The data says ₹2,900." And that was it.

Tuesday, 1 July. Joseph and Sahil have argued about the price of their tuition app for a week: ₹199 or ₹349 a month. Sahil slams his laptop shut. "We're going in circles." Joseph says, "Then let's stop guessing. Test both."
Wednesday, 2 July. They write the rules together. For three weeks, parents who sign up on odd dates see ₹199; parents on even dates see ₹349. The winner is whichever brings more paying parents who are still active after their first week. "Whatever it says, we follow it, even if it's you," Sahil says. They shake on it.
Wednesday, 23 July. The numbers: ₹349 brought fewer signups but nearly as many active parents, and more money. Joseph, who had wanted ₹199, winces, then laughs. "Fine. You win. The spreadsheet wins."

In Kumily, where their small spice-packing unit smelled of cardamom all day, Elizabeth and Sarita had stopped talking about anything except orders. The fight was about shares. Elizabeth had put in her savings; Sarita had found every farmer who supplied them. Each thought the other was asking for too much.
They went together to Varghese uncle, who had run a tea-trading business for thirty years. He sat them on his verandah with black tea and said, "Before you tell me what you want, tell me what she wants. And why."
Elizabeth struggled. "Sarita thinks her work built the supply, and without it my money would just sit in a bank." Sarita was slower. "Elizabeth thinks she took the risk. If we failed, she lost her savings, not me."
Varghese uncle nodded. "Good. Now you've both heard it. Here are three ways other people have split this."

Tariq cleared his throat. "Yara thinks the code is worthless without customers, and she got them." Yara said, "Tariq thinks the customers would never have signed without a product that worked."

Harish, most founders don't want to talk about breaking up on day one. It feels like planning a divorce at the wedding. I'm Anand, and my co-founder and I did it anyway, and I'm glad. We had both watched friends' startups fall apart: one ended in a legal notice, one where the founder who left after six months kept half the company.
So in our first month, while we still liked each other a lot, we sat with a startup lawyer and agreed on the basics. Shares would vest over four years, so you earn them by staying. And if one of us left, there was a fixed way to value the shares and buy them back.
Two years later, my co-founder did leave, for family reasons. It was sad. But nobody had to argue. We just opened the document and followed it.

I asked, "Who else does this, and why won't they crush you?" She talked for four minutes. Varun asked, "What does it cost you to get one customer, and what do they pay you over a year?" She guessed, then admitted she had guessed. I asked, "Why now? Why not five years ago?" Silence.

The customer numbers were real, from her sheet, including one she didn't like. For "why now" she said, "I'm not sure it's perfect timing; here's what changed last year."
I don't know how nervous she was at the real meetings. But her answers were short and honest.

Thursday. Jatin pitches his EV-charging startup to Vishal and Farida, two friends who have raised money before, in Vishal's living room. Vishal asks, "What's your margin on each charge?" Jatin says, "Healthy." Farida asks, "Why won't the big fuel companies just do this?" Jatin talks for five minutes and loses his own thread.
Sunday. Jatin sits with a notebook and rewrites. Margin: the actual number, from last month's data. Competition: "They will. Our edge is housing societies they don't want to bother with." Why now: "Two state subsidies changed in March." Each answer under thirty seconds.
Tuesday, the next week. Round two in the living room. Vishal repeats the margin question. Jatin gives the number and its weakness. Farida nods. "That I believe."

qa.q: What did Jatin first say about his margin?
qa.a: "Healthy."

qa.q: How did Jatin feel after losing his own thread on the competition question?
qa.a: Jatin likely felt flustered and embarrassed, which drove the careful rewriting on Sunday.

qa.q: What made the rewritten answers stronger?
qa.a: They used actual numbers, admitted weaknesses and stayed under thirty seconds.

qa.q: How does Farida react to the second round?
qa.a: Farida is convinced, saying "That I believe" once Jatin gives the real number and its weakness.

grounding: It shows a founder rehearsing with two experienced friends who probe competition, margins and timing, and rewriting answers until they are brief and honest.
